evidence.note: The soundtrack follows the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer). According to Wikipedia's article on the film, Gordon Zahler compiled the score from his late father Lee Zahler's stock-music library. Those compositions and recordings may have their own copyright histories. Check them before licensing the music for new synchronization or commercial release.

Ed Wood is credited as the film's creator on the Internet Archive item. We found nothing showing the film was adapted from an earlier published work, so the story takes the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer).
USPTO trademark databases could not be searched in this session. We know of no active mark for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space', but trademark status stays undetermined until a USPTO search is done.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions can be protected. The Internet Archive item includes a colourised version, and colorization can carry its own protection. Wikipedia reports that Turner Classic Movies released a high-definition transfer in 1.85:1 widescreen, with stock footage shots adjusted for framing, so such releases may add protectable material. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Plan 9 from Outer Space is a science-fiction horror film that Ed Wood made. Wikipedia reports that it was shot in November 1956 at Quality Studios in Los Angeles on a $60,000 budget. It previewed at the Carlton Theatre in Los Angeles on March 15, 1957, under the title Grave Robbers from Outer Space. General release began in July 1958, and the film was sold to television in 1961. Creators want it for its cult status as an alleged 'worst film ever made'. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.' but cites no registration or renewal search, and it marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'.

The rights trap is that nobody has shown the status with a primary record. We found no Copyright Office registration or renewal record, so the print stays undetermined. The soundtrack is also a compilation. Gordon Zahler assembled it from his late father Lee Zahler's stock-music library, and those tracks may have their own histories. The Internet Archive item carries a colourised version, which can be protected on its own, and Turner Classic Movies has released a widescreen high-definition transfer. Treat the film as unverified until a registration and renewal search is done, and get advice before reusing footage commercially.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.', but it cites no registration or renewal search, and we found no primary record either way. The status is undetermined until a Copyright Office search is done. Get advice before reusing footage commercially.
Does an Internet Archive copy or a Creative Commons label mean I can reuse it?

No. A hosting label on an uploaded copy does not decide the film's copyright status. The Public Domain Review marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'. Added material such as the colourised version or a new score can also be protected on its own.
